items.q: A user changes /api/orders/1001 to /api/orders/1002 and sees another customer's order. What is this flaw?
items.explanation: The server returned an object without checking that it belongs to the caller. That missing ownership check is BOLA, also called IDOR.

items.q: Where must authorization be enforced?
options: On the server, for every request
In the browser, by hiding buttons
items.explanation: Anything the client does can be skipped. The server must decide on every request whether this user may do this action on this object.

items.q: A user asks for an object they do not own. Which response is best?
options: A redirect to the home page
items.explanation: Return no data. A 404 can also avoid confirming that the object exists.

items.q: 'Deny by default' means:
options: Access is refused unless a rule grants it
Access is allowed unless a rule forbids it
items.explanation: New endpoints should be closed until someone explicitly grants access, so a forgotten check fails safe.

items.q: Random, hard-to-guess IDs instead of 1, 2, 3 ...
options: Only make enumeration harder; the server-side ownership check is still required
Are slower to index, so avoid them
items.explanation: Unguessable IDs are good hygiene, but an attacker who obtains one ID (from a log, a link, a colleague) still gets the data unless the server checks ownership.

items.q: A normal user calls POST /admin/users directly. No page links to it. What is the right fix?
options: Check the caller's role on the server for that endpoint
items.explanation: Hidden is not protected. The endpoint itself must check the role (function-level authorization).

items.q: Mass assignment is when:
options: A request's fields are bound straight onto a model, so a user can send role=admin
Many users log in at once
items.explanation: Bind only an explicit allow-list of fields; never copy the whole request body onto a model.

items.q: Which is appropriate for storing passwords?
options: argon2id or bcrypt with a per-password salt
items.explanation: Password hashes must be slow and salted. argon2id, bcrypt and scrypt are built for that; fast hashes let attackers test billions of guesses per second.

items.q: Why is MD5 unsuitable for security uses?
options: Practical collisions exist and it is extremely fast to brute-force
items.explanation: MD5 collisions can be produced cheaply, and its speed helps password cracking.

items.q: AES in ECB mode is a problem because:
options: Identical plaintext blocks give identical ciphertext blocks, leaking patterns
items.explanation: ECB encrypts every block independently. Use an authenticated mode such as AES-GCM.

items.q: Reusing a nonce with the same key in AES-GCM:
options: Can break both confidentiality and authentication
items.explanation: Every message needs a unique nonce for a given key. Generate it randomly (96-bit) or with a counter you never repeat.

items.q: Which is a suitable source of randomness for session tokens?
options: The operating system's CSPRNG (secrets, crypto.randomBytes, SecureRandom)
items.explanation: General-purpose random generators are predictable. Tokens must come from a cryptographically secure generator.

items.q: Hard-coding an encryption key in source code:
options: Is safe if the repository is private
Exposes it to anyone with the code or its history; keep keys in a secret store
items.explanation: Keys in code end up in repositories, builds and logs. Load them from a secret manager or the environment, and rotate them.

items.q: Which setting protects data in transit?
options: TLS 1.2 or newer with a valid certificate
items.explanation: Encoding is not encryption. Use TLS with certificate validation turned on.

items.q: What is the best fix for SQL injection?
items.explanation: With parameters the database receives the query and the data separately, so input can never change the query's structure.

items.q: A login form receives ' OR '1'='1 as the username. The attacker is trying to:
options: Make the WHERE clause always true
items.explanation: If the input is concatenated into the query, the condition becomes always true and the login check passes.

items.q: os.system('ping ' + host) is vulnerable to:
items.explanation: A value such as '8.8.8.8; cat /etc/passwd' runs a second command through the shell.

items.q: What is the safer way to run an external program?
options: Build a command string for the shell
Pass an argument list and no shell
items.explanation: subprocess.run([...]), execFile, ProcessBuilder(list) and exec.Command(name, args...) do not go through a shell, so metacharacters stay plain text.

items.q: Is a blocklist of 'bad characters' a sufficient defence?
options: Yes, if written as a regex
No; it misses encodings and variants. Use parameterization and allow-lists
items.explanation: Attackers find the character or encoding you forgot. Remove the interpreter from the data path instead.

items.q: An ORM protects against SQL injection:
options: Only when you use its parameter binding, not when you concatenate raw SQL into it
items.explanation: Raw-query escape hatches (raw(), text(), nativeQuery) are as injectable as hand-written SQL if you build them with string joins.

items.q: Which is an example of NoSQL injection?
options: Sending a JSON object such as {"$ne": null} where a string was expected
items.explanation: If the server passes request JSON straight into a query, operators like $ne or $gt change its meaning. Validate types and reject objects.

items.q: Which is a security misconfiguration?
items.explanation: Debug mode often exposes stack traces, interactive consoles and configuration.

items.q: An API key was committed to Git and removed in a later commit. The key is now:
options: Still in the history, so it must be rotated
items.explanation: Deleting a file does not delete history or forks. Treat the key as leaked and rotate it.

items.q: Where should secrets live?
options: In the environment or a secret manager, not in the repository
items.explanation: Anything in code or the browser is readable by whoever gets the code or the page.

items.q: Default admin credentials left unchanged are:
items.explanation: Default credentials are published. Change them at install time, or generate unique ones.

items.q: Detailed error pages with stack traces should:
options: Not be shown; return a generic message and log the details on the server
items.explanation: Stack traces reveal file paths, library versions and queries that guide an attacker.

items.q: A Content-Security-Policy header helps by:
options: Restricting what the browser may load or run
items.explanation: CSP limits script, style and frame sources, which reduces the impact of injected content.

items.q: Directory listing enabled on a web server may:
options: Expose files that were never meant to be public
items.explanation: Backups, configs and source files show up when the server lists a folder. Turn listing off.

items.q: What is an SBOM?
options: A list of the components and versions inside your software
items.explanation: A software bill of materials lets you answer 'do we use library X, and which version?' quickly.

items.q: What is the most reliable way to learn you use a vulnerable library?
options: Scan manifests and lockfiles against vulnerability databases on a schedule
items.explanation: Automated, repeated scanning (OSV, Trivy, npm audit, pip-audit, govulncheck) catches new advisories for old dependencies.

items.q: A lockfile is useful because it:
options: Pins exact versions so builds are reproducible and auditable
items.explanation: What you test is what you ship, and a scanner knows exactly which versions to check.

items.q: A transitive dependency is:
options: A dependency of one of your dependencies
items.explanation: Most vulnerable code arrives indirectly. Scanners must read the full resolved tree, not just your top-level list.

items.q: CVE-2021-44228 ('Log4Shell') was in which library?
items.explanation: It affected Apache Log4j2's JNDI lookups.

items.q: Typosquatting is when:
options: A malicious package uses a name similar to a popular one
items.explanation: Check names carefully and prefer lockfiles, private registries or allow-lists.

items.q: No fixed version of a vulnerable dependency exists. A reasonable response is:
options: Mitigate (disable the feature, restrict exposure) or replace it, and track the risk
items.explanation: Reduce exposure now and plan the replacement.

items.q: Which control slows down password guessing?
options: Telling the user which field was wrong
Rate limiting with lockout or back-off
items.explanation: Limit attempts per account and per source, and add increasing delays.

items.q: Different messages for 'user not found' and 'wrong password' allow:
options: User enumeration: attackers learn which usernames exist
items.explanation: Use one generic message and equal response time for both cases.

items.q: A JWT is read with jwt.decode() and no signature check. This is:
options: Forgeable: anyone can write their own claims
items.explanation: decode() only parses. Always call the verify function with the expected algorithms and key.

items.q: After a successful login you should:
options: Issue a new session ID to prevent fixation
Put the session ID in the URL
items.explanation: A fresh session ID defeats an attacker who planted a known ID before login.

items.q: Multi-factor authentication helps because:
options: A stolen password alone is no longer enough
items.explanation: A second factor stops most credential-stuffing and phishing-for-password attacks.

items.q: Comparing secrets with == can leak information through timing. Use:
items.explanation: hmac.compare_digest, crypto.timingSafeEqual, MessageDigest.isEqual and subtle.ConstantTimeCompare compare in constant time.

items.q: Which cookie attributes should a session cookie have?
items.explanation: Secure keeps it on HTTPS, HttpOnly hides it from scripts, SameSite limits cross-site sending.

items.q: SSRF happens when:
options: A server fetches a URL chosen by the user and can be steered to internal targets
items.explanation: The server's network position (inside the firewall, with cloud credentials) is borrowed by the attacker.

items.q: Which target is the classic SSRF prize in a cloud environment?
items.explanation: It can hand out temporary credentials for the machine's role.

items.q: What is the best defence?
options: An allow-list of destinations plus refusing private and link-local addresses after DNS resolution
items.explanation: Blocklists of names are bypassed with other spellings and encodings of the same address.

items.q: Why check the IP address after DNS resolution?
options: A public-looking hostname can resolve to an internal address, or change between checks (DNS rebinding)
items.explanation: Validate the address you will actually connect to, and connect to that address.

items.q: Following redirects automatically is risky because:
options: An allowed host can redirect to an internal one
items.explanation: Disable redirects, or re-validate every hop.

items.q: Blind SSRF means:
options: The attacker cannot see the screen
The response is not shown but the server still makes the request, so you detect it with an out-of-band callback
items.explanation: A callback listener that records an incoming request is the usual proof.

items.q: Which URL schemes should a fetch-by-URL feature usually refuse?
items.explanation: Allow only http and https. file://, gopher:// and others reach local files or raw sockets.

items.q: Cross-site scripting lets an attacker:
options: Run script in other users' browsers on your site
items.explanation: The injected script runs with the page's privileges: it can read the page, act as the user and send data away.

items.q: What is the best primary defence?
items.explanation: Encode data for the place it lands: HTML body, attribute, JavaScript string or URL each need their own encoding.

items.q: element.innerHTML = userInput is dangerous because:
options: The browser parses the input as HTML
items.explanation: Use textContent (or a framework's escaped binding) to insert text.

items.q: A Content-Security-Policy:
options: Adds defence in depth by limiting where scripts may come from
items.explanation: CSP is a second layer. Encoding stays the first.

items.q: Stored XSS differs from reflected XSS because:
options: Stored XSS only affects the client
Stored XSS persists on the server and hits every viewer; reflected XSS needs the victim to open a crafted link
items.explanation: Stored XSS in a comment or profile field is usually the more serious of the two.

items.q: HttpOnly cookies help because:
options: Scripts cannot read them, so XSS cannot simply steal the session
items.explanation: XSS can still act as the user, but it cannot copy the cookie value to another machine.

items.q: In a template engine, which is the safest default?
options: Marking user input as 'safe' or raw
items.explanation: Keep auto-escaping on. Treat every |safe, Markup(), v-html, dangerouslySetInnerHTML and template.HTML as a review item.
